newsitem.title: USA: U.S. Treasuries open higher before jobless claims.
newsitem.headline: U.S. Treasuries open higher before jobless claims.

text.p: U.S. government securities prices opened higher on Thursday ahead of the government's weekly release on new jobless claims.
The Labor Department will report figures on new claims for state unemployment insurance at 0830 EDT/1230 GMT.
Economists polled by Reuters estimated, on average, that those claims totaled 307,000 for the week ended August 2, up from 277,000 a week earlier.
In early dealings, the benchmark 30-year Treasury bond was up 3/32 to 101-31/32, yielding 6.47 percent.
Analysts said the market's primary focus is on the Treasury's $10.0 billion 30-year bond sale, the last leg of the Treasury's three-part refunding effort.
"No doubt (the focus is) the auction," said Kevin Flanagan, first vice president and money market economist at Dean Witter Reynolds.

Flanagan said in contrast to the first two parts of the auction, the Treasury's sale of $16.0 billion in three-year notes on Tuesday and the sale of $12.0 billion in 10-year notes on Wednesday, some economic data will be released prior to the 1300 EDT/1700 GMT bidding deadline for the 30-years.
Flanagan called the jobless claims data "a wild card what with auto plant shutdowns for retooling and vacations" affecting the data.
June wholesale inventory data, for which no forecast was available, are also due at 1000 EDT/1400 GMT.
Flanagan said the market had found good support at 6.50 percent on the 30-year bond yield and 6.25 percent on the 10-year note yield.
He said those would be strong support levels for the foreseeable future until there is some "smoking gun" on inflation.
If July retail sales, producer and consumer price data next week are benign, said Flanagan, yields could decline from current levels.
Flanagan said he estimated that the 30-year bonds to be auctioned this afternoon would be sold with an average yield of 6.45 percent to 6.48 percent.
In early trade, the 30-year bonds were yielding 6.445 percent on a when-issued basis.
At the short end of the maturity range, three-, six- and year bill rates were unchanged at 5.14 percent, 5.20 percent and 5.22 percent, respectively.
The two-year Treasury note was up 1/32 to 99-31/32 to yield 5.89 percent.
The five-year note was up 2/32 to 99-20/32 to yield 6.09 percent.
Ten-year notes were priced at 99-18/32, yielding 6.18 percent.
